generated_by: PHP refusals are exercised by prism:tests/ValueObjects/Media/FetchGuardCorpusTest.php. The TypeScript and Python columns were recorded by executing their guarded fetch methods against the shipped loader rows with injected DNS and HTTP seams. Python skips url-0009 because no unguarded media fetch exists by design.

cases.title: a genuinely public host
cases.notes: The control. Every refusal row below is noise until this one fetches: a guard that refuses everything passes them all.

cases.title: the cloud metadata endpoint
cases.notes: The address this guard exists for: it hands role credentials to anything inside the network that asks. Link-local, so the literal check alone refuses it.

cases.title: a loopback literal
cases.notes: Refuse loopback literals before making a request to a service on the caller's own machine.

cases.title: an IPv6 loopback literal
cases.notes: Bracketed, so a port that forgets to strip the brackets before validating reads it as a hostname and tries to resolve it â€” which is how an IPv6 hole opens in a guard that closed the IPv4 one.

cases.title: an RFC 1918 literal
cases.notes: Refuse private IPv4 literals so public media fetching cannot reach internal network services.

cases.title: a public NAME that resolves to a private address
cases.notes: The bypass a URL-string check misses entirely: the attacker owns the DNS record, so the host looks public and the connection is internal. A port that validates only the literal passes every row above this one and fails here.

cases.title: a name answering with one public and one private address
cases.notes: EVERY resolved address is checked, not the first. A host answering with both reaches the private one, and a port that stops at the first record reads this as public.

cases.title: a public host redirecting into the metadata endpoint
cases.notes: A DIFFERENT code from the address refusals, and deliberately so: the caller's input was fine and the server aimed them somewhere internal. Redirects are followed by default in every HTTP client here, so a port that validates only the URL it was handed makes the internal request and never knows.

cases.title: the UNGUARDED fetch still fetches a loopback address
cases.notes: PHP and TypeScript preserve their pre-existing unguarded fetch methods. Python has no unguarded media fetch by design and skips this legacy-path control; adding one would introduce an SSRF-capable path solely to make the corpus greener.

skip.py: Python has no unguarded fetch method by design; there is no legacy path to assert.

cases.title: a non-http scheme
cases.notes: Handed to an HTTP client that would happily read the file. Refused before any address check, because there is no address to check.

cases.title: a host that resolves to nothing
cases.notes: An empty answer must mean "could not be verified", never "nothing to check". A port that treats no records as a pass turns every DNS failure into an allowed fetch.

cases.title: a public host redirecting forever
cases.notes: Six requests pin the default redirect-hop allowance at five in PHP, TypeScript and Python: the initial request plus five allowed hops are sent, then too_many_redirects must be raised before a seventh request. A language that defaults to three would refuse under the same code but fail this six-request assertion. Every response redirects even when already at redirects_to; no hop serves content.

cases.title: Alibaba Cloud's metadata endpoint, in CGNAT
cases.notes: G-89. 100.64.0.0/10 is shared address space, not private: filter_var's private and reserved flags admit it, and so did the ranges copied from them. All three languages admitted this until the explicit list.

cases.title: the NAT64 spelling of 169.254.169.254
cases.notes: G-89. On an IPv6-only network with NAT64 this IS the metadata endpoint. The guard judges the IPv4 address embedded in 64:ff9b::/96, not the IPv6 wrapper.

cases.title: the 6to4 spelling of 169.254.169.254
cases.notes: G-89. 2002::/16 embeds an IPv4 address in bits 16-48; judged by that address.

cases.title: a public NAME whose DNS answer is the NAT64 metadata address
cases.notes: G-89. The literal rows prove the check; this one proves the check runs on every DNS answer too, where an attacker who owns the record chooses the spelling.

cases.title: a public name answered with NAT64 of a PUBLIC address still fetches
cases.notes: G-89's control. A DNS64 resolver hands an IPv6-only host 64:ff9b:: addresses for public sites (this is 93.184.216.34). A guard that refused NAT64 outright would pass url-0014 and url-0016 and break every fetch on such a network; this row fails it.
